why:
Both the mass number and the atomic number must balance across a nuclear reaction.

Mass number: \(27 + 4 = 31\) on the left, so the two products must add to 31. The neutron carries 1, leaving \(31 - 1 = 30\) for the missing nuclide.

Atomic number: \(13 + 2 = 15\) on the left. The neutron carries 0, so the missing nuclide has \(Z = 15\), which is phosphorus.

The missing particle is therefore \(^{30}_{15}\mathrm{P}\), and the balanced reaction is \(^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \longrightarrow {}^{30}_{15}\mathrm{P} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\).

Why each of the other three fails: \(^{32}_{16}\mathrm{S}\) has \(A = 32\) and \(Z = 16\), so both sums overshoot (they would need a left-hand side of 33 and 16). \(^{14}_{10}\mathrm{Ne}\) has \(A = 14\) and \(Z = 10\), which balances neither. The last choice is printed as \(_{14}\mathrm{Si}\) with no mass number at all, and its atomic number 14 is one short of the required 15, so it cannot balance the charge either.
solution: [Textbook misprint: alternative (d) is printed as \(_{14}\mathrm{Si}\), with an atomic number but no mass number. It is wrong either way, since balancing the reaction requires \(Z = 15\), but as printed it cannot even be tested against the mass-number balance.]

why:
The decay constant and the half life are related by \(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\).

Here \(t_{1/2} = 5.27\ \mathrm{y}\), so

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{5.27\ \mathrm{y}} = 0.1315\ \mathrm{y^{-1}} \approx 0.132\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\).

Why each of the other three fails: 0.138 is printed with no unit and in any case is not \(0.693/5.27\); 29.6 y carries the unit of TIME, whereas a decay constant is a fraction decaying per unit time and must have the unit \(\mathrm{y^{-1}}\); and 13.8 % is a pure percentage, which again is not a rate constant.

why:
Table 13.4 (b) of this chapter lists the therapeutic radioisotopes and the disease each one treats. Against phosphorus (half life 14 days, a beta emitter) it prints the use "treatment of leukemia", so the isotope is \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\).

Why each of the other three fails: the same table gives \(^{60}\mathrm{Co}\) (half life 5.3 years) as an EXTERNAL radiation source for cancer treatment, not for leukemia; it gives \(^{226}\mathrm{Ra}\) (half life 1620 years) as an isotope implanted in tumours; and \(^{226}\mathrm{I}\) appears nowhere in the chapter at all — the therapeutic iodine isotope the table does list is \(^{131}\mathrm{I}\), used for thyroid cancer.

Section 13.7.5 defines nuclear fusion as the process in which "the lighter nuclei combine (fuse) together and form a heavy nucleus which is accompanied by an enormous amount of energy". That is exactly the process described in the stem, so the answer is nuclear fusion.

Why each of the other three fails: a chemical reaction involves only the rearrangement of atoms through the outer-shell electrons (Table 13.3) and leaves every nucleus unchanged, so it cannot build a heavier nucleus. Nuclear fission is the opposite process — section 13.7.3 defines it as the SPLITTING of a heavy nucleus into two nearly equal fragments. A chain reaction is not a way of joining nuclei at all; it is the self-sustaining sequence in which the neutrons released by one fission trigger further fissions.
